projects.name: Debt Ledger
projects.title: Make the balance explainable.
projects.deck: A debt-tracking product needs a clear relationship between what the user sees and what the system records. My work connected the journey, the business logic, and the path to release.
fields: User journeys, business logic, delivery alignment
Shipped in two months across four sprints
Debt accounts, payment history, QR payment request

sections.title: Domain context
sections.body:
Debt tracking connects a relationship with a record: who owes an amount, what has been paid, and what remains. That record needs to stay understandable when events do not arrive in a neat sequence. A partial payment, a repeated notification, or a later correction can change what the product needs to explain.

My work on Debt Ledger covered discovery through delivery, mapping user journeys into business logic and helping resolve cross-functional bottlenecks. The product shipped in two months across four sprints. The part of that work I want to make visible is how a journey becomes precise enough for different people to discuss the same behavior.

sections.title: The product question
sections.body:
**How do you make debt tracking clear enough to use and precise enough to implement?**

A debt balance represents several events: an amount owed, a payment, and sometimes a correction. The useful experience connects those events so someone can understand the remaining amount and see the records behind it.

The challenge was to translate that workflow into an automated debt-tracking product within a short delivery window. A polished overview alone would not resolve the underlying questions about how the workflow should behave.

sections.title: What I owned
sections.body:
I owned the discovery-to-delivery lifecycle. I mapped user journeys and translated them into business logic, helping resolve cross-functional bottlenecks and maintain alignment through delivery.

My contribution was the connection between the user's task and the behavior the team needed to implement. The product shipped in two months across four sprints.

sections.title: From the journey to the rules
sections.body:
The product views connect debt accounts, transaction history, and a QR payment request. They represent connected parts of the workflow:

1. Understand what is owed.
2. Inspect the records associated with the balance.
3. Request or record a payment.
4. Understand the resulting status and remaining amount.

Mapping that relationship matters because every visible action implies a business rule. A payment action needs a definition of when the payment is recognized. A history view needs to explain the event. A balance needs to remain consistent with the records that support it.

This is the kind of detail I want to make explicit when moving from discovery into implementation.

sections.title: Decision notes
sections.body: Looking back at the choices behind the experience.

sections.title: Looking back — the decisions I would make explicit
sections.body:
**1. Define what is allowed to change the balance.**

A useful starting point is to separate a payment request from a confirmed payment. A QR code can provide payment context; it cannot, by itself, establish that money arrived. I would define the confirmation source and the rules for applying a payment with the technical and business owners.

**2. Give exceptions a visible route.**

Partial payments, repeated notifications, unmatched payments, and reversals raise different questions. I would specify the expected behavior for each before treating automation as complete. Where a payment cannot be matched confidently, a visible review state gives the team a way to resolve uncertainty.

**3. Preserve an explanation when something changes.**

If a recorded payment is corrected or reversed, I would preserve a traceable relationship to the original event. The user should be able to understand the new balance without losing the history that explains it.

These are retrospective design and analysis principles. They describe how I would make the product more explicit; they are not a claim that every example below shipped in the initial release.

sections.title: A small illustration of the thinking
sections.body:
Start with VND 1,000,000 owed. Select each event to see how the balance and review queue relate.

This illustrates the reasoning. It is not a description of every rule shipped in the original release.

sections.title: The delivery result
sections.body:
The product shipped in two months across four sprints. My work covered discovery, journey mapping, business logic, and delivery alignment.

That milestone demonstrates delivery. To judge the product's continuing value, I would look separately at adoption, reconciliation effort, and the reliability of the resulting records.

sections.title: What I would measure next
sections.body:
| Question | Measure I would define |
| --- | --- |
| Does it reduce operating effort? | Time needed to reconcile a comparable workload |
| Is the automation useful? | Correctly matched eligible payments, with incorrect matches tracked separately |
| Can users trust the record? | Balance corrections and unresolved exceptions per defined transaction volume |
| Does it become part of routine work? | Continued meaningful ledger use by a defined merchant cohort |

I would inspect the most frequent exceptions before adding more features. If people spend their time correcting or explaining a balance, that is a concrete place to investigate.

sections.title: Personal reflection
sections.body:
**Every number should have a story the system can explain.**

For me, this is where business analysis becomes tangible. The balance, the history, and the available action need to describe the same situation. Making that relationship explicit gives the team a better basis for implementation and gives the user a clearer record to work with.

projects.description: Connecting debt-tracking journeys with business logic and delivery, with a release shipped in two months across four sprints.

decisions.question: What should be allowed to change the outstanding balance?
decisions.options: Treat a payment request as sufficient; rely on a person to confirm every change; or define a trusted confirmation event and send uncertain cases to review.
decisions.reasoning: I would separate the request from the evidence that payment occurred. I would also give repeated events and corrections explicit rules, so the same payment cannot silently change the balance twice and a correction retains an explanation.
decisions.check: Walk through complete examples with business and technical colleagues. For each event, compare the balance, the history, and the action available to the user. Then evaluate real reconciliation effort and exception patterns after release.

projects.name: mSeller
projects.title: Make the next action obvious.
projects.deck: Merchant software needs to fit the work happening around it. My contribution combined business analysis and UI/UX design to simplify core actions and connect onboarding with the payment experience.
fields: Merchant operations, illustrated through restaurant workflows
Interface simplification, guided onboarding, early dynamic QR integration

sections.title: Domain context
sections.body:
Merchant operations connect several states that need to remain understandable: which table or order is active, what still needs attention, and whether payment is complete. The interface is one part of that operating context. Its hierarchy needs to support the person doing the work at the moment they need it.

I am interested in the connection between a business process and the action the screen makes prominent. In mSeller, my business analysis and UI/UX work included simplifying core flows around one or two primary actions, guided onboarding, and early dynamic QR integration. The important question behind that simplification is whether the person still has enough context to choose correctly.

sections.title: The product question
sections.body:
**How can software help staff move through a task without repeatedly making them interpret the interface?**

The presented workflows move between table status, orders, shift setup, and payment. Each moment has a different immediate purpose. An interface that gives everything the same visual priority makes that purpose harder to recognize.

My objective was to simplify the operating experience by making the relevant action easier to identify.

sections.title: What I contributed
sections.body:
As Lead Business Analyst and UI/UX Designer, I simplified the interface and organized core flows around one or two primary actions. I also worked on early dynamic QR integration and created custom animated onboarding to guide key interactions.

The action count describes visual priority. It is not a claim that every merchant task was completed in two taps.

sections.title: The connection between workflow and interface
sections.body:
A table overview supports a different decision from an order detail or payment screen. Business analysis helps establish what that decision is; interface hierarchy helps make it visible.

For me, this is the valuable connection between the two disciplines. A primary action should be the natural next step in a well-understood workflow. It should not have to compensate for an unclear process.

sections.title: Decision notes
sections.body: Looking back at the choices behind the experience.

sections.title: Looking back — three trade-offs behind a simple flow
sections.body:
**1. Immediate clarity versus access to less common actions.**

Fewer prominent controls can make the next step easier to recognize, but secondary actions still need a discoverable home. I would examine whether staff can complete the routine task quickly and recover when they need a less common option.

**2. Guidance for a new user versus speed for a returning user.**

Animated onboarding can explain an unfamiliar interaction. In repeated work, the same instruction can become an interruption. I would keep the explanation dismissible, make help easy to revisit, and evaluate whether the guidance actually improves task completion.

**3. A payment request versus a completed payment.**

Entering the payment flow is different from receiving confirmation. I would agree with engineering and payment partners on the evidence required to mark an order paid, then design the pending, unsuccessful, and recovery states around that rule.

These are the questions I would bring to a review of the next iteration.

sections.title: Questions for the next product review
sections.body:
- A payment request, an attempted payment, and confirmed receipt need distinguishable states.
- Canceling or changing an order raises permission and history questions.
- Repeated taps or a delayed response need behavior that avoids accidental duplication.
- Onboarding should remain dismissible and accessible again when needed.

sections.title: The contribution and the evidence
sections.body:
My contribution combined workflow analysis, simpler primary actions, animated onboarding, and early dynamic QR integration. The screens make that design work visible.

To establish the size of the improvement, I would compare the same task across interface versions and observe completion, errors, hesitation, and assistance needed. A reduction in visible controls alone cannot establish a reduction in task time or support effort.

sections.title: What I would measure next
sections.body:
| Question | Measure I would define |
| --- | --- |
| Can a new merchant reach first value? | First successful order or payment within a defined onboarding window |
| Does the interface help routine work? | Task completion, median task time, and assistance needed |
| Is payment status understandable? | Correct interpretation of pending, confirmed, and unsuccessful states |
| Is use sustained? | Continued transacting activity by a defined merchant cohort |

I would also examine payment exceptions and support contacts. An easier first experience needs to remain dependable during repeated use.

sections.title: Personal reflection
sections.body:
**A clear next action depends on a clear understanding of the work.**

I enjoy merchant products because the details have an immediate purpose. The interface has to communicate what is happening and help someone continue. My strongest interest is the reasoning behind that apparent simplicity: understanding the flow, choosing the priority, and keeping the visible status consistent with the underlying behavior.

projects.description: Simplifying merchant workflows through clear primary actions, guided onboarding, and payment context.

decisions.question: How much should a merchant screen ask someone to consider at once?
decisions.options: Show every operation as a primary control; emphasize the immediate task and reveal secondary actions in context; or provide different views for different operating responsibilities.
decisions.reasoning: I would give the immediate task a strong visual priority while preserving a discoverable route to less common actions. A simplified screen still needs to identify the order, the amount, and the relevant status. Hiding necessary context would make the interface harder to trust.
decisions.check: Observe the same task with new and returning users. Look at completion, wrong selections, hesitation, and the ability to recover after a mistake.

projects.name: BeeRich
projects.title: Help the next financial decision make sense.
projects.deck: A financial overview should help someone understand their position and see a useful next step. My contribution connected personal finance with banking services and championed a unified dashboard.
fields: Personal finance integration with banking services; unified dashboard direction
Savings, spending visibility, and investment information

sections.title: Domain context
sections.body:
Personal finance brings several kinds of information into one experience. Spending describes what has happened. Savings relates to an intention or a commitment. Investment information introduces another set of expectations about value and availability. Bringing those views together is useful only if their meaning remains clear.

The product question that interests me is how an overview can help someone orient themselves before taking an action. I would start with the decision the person is trying to make and work backward to the information required. That changes the conversation from “How many features fit on the dashboard?” to “What deserves attention first?”

sections.title: The product question
sections.body:
**How do you bring financial information together without making the overview harder to understand?**

Personal finance involves several related questions: what someone has, where money goes, how saving is progressing, and what financial action might be relevant. An app can display each answer separately while leaving the user to connect them.

The opportunity was to make the relationship between those views easier to understand within a connected banking experience.

sections.title: What I contributed
sections.body:
As Product Owner and Analyst, I worked on integrating personal finance management with banking services. I championed a unified dashboard to organize the experience and reduce unnecessary cognitive effort.

My contribution focused on product definition and the connection between financial information and available actions. The savings, spending, and investment views illustrate that direction.

sections.title: The experience direction
sections.body:
A unified overview can provide a useful starting point when its hierarchy is clear. Savings progress, spending information, and investment content each need a purpose in that first view.

The design question is what someone should understand first and how the experience helps them move into detail. A dashboard becomes more useful when it gives the information a relationship to an actual decision.

sections.title: Decision notes
sections.body: Looking back at the choices behind the experience.

sections.title: Looking back — three decisions worth evaluating
sections.body:
**1. Begin with a recurring decision.**

I would identify a specific question the overview should help answer, then choose the information needed for it. That keeps the hierarchy grounded in a user task rather than a list of available banking products.

**2. Make the meaning of each figure clear.**

An available balance, a historical spending total, and an investment valuation have different meanings. I would check whether users understand those differences, including the relevant time period and whether a figure may be delayed.

**3. Keep the next action relevant.**

A promotional card can attract attention, but its usefulness depends on the surrounding context. I would evaluate whether people understand why an action is relevant before treating its click rate as a success.

These questions describe how I would evaluate the next iteration.

sections.title: The main trade-off
sections.body:
**Breadth of information versus depth of understanding.**

Putting more information in the overview offers convenience, but it also increases reading effort. A more focused overview needs a clear route to the details that some users require.

I would test whether people can identify and explain the information needed for a realistic task. That would give the team a stronger basis for choosing the hierarchy than visual preference alone.

sections.title: Questions for the next product review
sections.body:
- How does the interface distinguish available funds from an investment valuation?
- How is a missing or delayed data source explained?
- Can someone find the period behind a spending summary?
- Does an action communicate its conditions before asking for commitment?

sections.title: The contribution and the evidence
sections.body:
My contribution covered personal-finance integration and the unified-dashboard direction. The screens illustrate the experience.

To connect that work to a business outcome, I would define the eligible users, the financial action that represents activation, and the period over which continued use is evaluated. Product reach and personal contribution should remain distinguishable.

sections.title: What I would measure next
sections.body:
| Question | Measure I would define |
| --- | --- |
| Do people understand the overview? | Correctly interpreting the relevant figures in a realistic task |
| Do they reach meaningful value? | A defined first financial action by eligible new users |
| Does the product remain useful? | Meaningful return activity in a consistent cohort window |
| Does engagement translate into financial behavior? | Repeat contributions or funded actions, separate from views and clicks |

I would assess comprehension and task completion before interpreting engagement as evidence of financial clarity.

sections.title: Personal reflection
sections.body:
**A dashboard earns its place by helping someone understand.**

What I find interesting about financial UX is that clarity requires both information design and respect for the meaning of the data. My contribution to BeeRich connected personal finance with banking services and championed a unified dashboard. Looking back, I would judge that direction by the quality of the understanding it creates, alongside the actions it enables.

projects.description: Connecting personal finance with banking services through a unified dashboard and a clearer information hierarchy.

decisions.question: What should a unified financial overview prioritize?
decisions.options: Give savings, spending, and investment equal prominence; lead with a smaller set of useful summaries; or personalize the hierarchy using information the product can responsibly interpret.
decisions.reasoning: I would begin with a clear shared hierarchy and an understandable route into detail. Personalization becomes useful when the underlying data and intent are reliable enough to support it. The overview should help someone interpret their position without implying that every displayed amount is equally available to spend.
decisions.check: Ask people to explain the main figures in their own words and complete a realistic task. Watch for confusion about time period, amount type, and the effect of the next action.

projects.name: Moodify
projects.title: Make room for a calmer first step.
projects.line: Make room for a calmer first step.
projects.description: An experience design study connecting a gentle introduction, meditation content, practitioner discovery, and a personal wellbeing overview.
projects.deck: Moodify explores how a wellbeing experience can bring together a gentle introduction, self-guided meditation, practitioner discovery, and a personal overview. The product question is how to offer a useful direction while leaving the person in control of what comes next.
fields: Product thinking, user journeys, and interface design
Onboarding, meditation discovery, practitioner profile, and dashboard
annotations: A clear invitation leaves room to choose.
Trust depends on understanding who, what, and what happens next.
The overview should help someone choose one useful direction.

sections.title: Domain context
sections.body:
A wellbeing product can become another source of decisions if its first experience is too demanding. The design challenge I want to explore is how to introduce useful possibilities without asking someone to explain everything about themselves before beginning.

The Moodify screens bring together several different intentions: finding a quiet activity, exploring content, considering a conversation, and returning to a personal overview. Those intentions need clear relationships. A welcoming visual style helps establish a tone, while the navigation has to explain what the person can actually do.

sections.title: The product question
sections.body:
**How can a wellbeing app help someone choose a manageable next step without making the experience feel like a test?**

My starting point is a small, understandable choice. The person should be able to see the available direction, understand what it involves, and decide whether it suits the moment. That gives me a more concrete design question than trying to make every part of the experience feel universally calming.

sections.title: The scope of this case
sections.body:
This case focuses on the presented interface flow and the reasoning I would use to develop it further: how onboarding sets expectations, how content becomes discoverable, what a practitioner profile needs to explain, and how a dashboard can support a return visit.

The screens are the design material. The decision notes describe the product questions and evaluation choices I would bring to the next iteration.

sections.title: The experience journey
sections.body:
**1. An invitation to enter**

The forest entrance and restrained brand treatment create a visual pause. I would keep that atmosphere while making the first action clear and immediate. Someone returning to the app should be able to reach useful content without repeatedly waiting through an introduction.

**2. A short, optional introduction**

The three onboarding screens introduce emotional awareness, meditation, and connection through imagery. My next step would be to give each panel one clear promise and a specific action. Skip and back controls help preserve choice while the person is still learning what the app offers.

**3. A useful personal overview**

The dashboard groups Relaxing, Connect, Sound, Learn, and Feelings. I would examine whether these labels help someone choose or leave them guessing about overlapping categories. A useful overview should make it easy to find one relevant activity and return to something familiar.

**4. A route into self-guided content**

The meditation screen introduces categories and a Counting Breaths card. Before starting an activity, I would want the person to understand what it involves, how long it takes, and whether audio is required. Those details belong to the next content-design iteration; the current board does not establish a completed session experience.

**5. A considered route to connection**

The profile view brings together personal information, services, reviews, and meeting/message actions. That makes trust and expectation-setting central to the flow. I would want a person to understand the practitioner’s role, relevant qualifications, language, availability, and the next step before sharing personal information or sending a request.

sections.title: Decision notes
sections.body: Questions I would bring to the next iteration.

sections.title: Exceptions and boundaries
sections.body:
I would make the next iteration explicit about the moments where an expectation could be broken: content that cannot load, an interrupted activity, an unavailable practitioner, or a meeting request that has not been accepted.

A request needs its own status. A message needs a realistic response expectation. Personal reflection should have understandable choices about what is stored and who can see it. The experience should also be clear about the limits of the service it provides.

These are design questions for the next iteration. They are not claims that the current screens represent a clinical service or a completed support workflow.

sections.title: What the work shows
sections.body:
The presented screens establish an experience direction: a visual welcome, a short introduction, routes into self-guided content and connection, and a dashboard for returning to the product.

The next step would be to test whether those parts form an understandable journey. I would look for evidence that someone can choose a direction, explain what will happen next, and navigate back without assistance.

sections.title: What I would evaluate next
sections.body:
| Learning question | Evidence I would seek |
| --- | --- |
| Is the beginning understandable? | Whether someone can explain the offer after the introduction and select a first action. |
| Are the categories distinct? | Whether people choose the expected category for a realistic task and explain that choice. |
| Does the content set expectations? | Whether someone can explain the activity, duration, and controls before starting. |
| Does the profile answer trust questions? | What remains unclear before a person considers contacting the practitioner. |
| Does the dashboard support a return visit? | Whether someone can find a previous activity and understand what the indicators represent. |

I would combine task observation with open questions about comfort and clarity. Time spent and repeat visits may describe use; they do not establish an improvement in wellbeing.

sections.title: Personal reflection
sections.body:
**Calm begins with giving someone room to choose.**

Moodify is interesting to me because it changes the tone of the product question. In a merchant workflow, I might emphasize the next operational action. Here, I want the next step to feel understandable without becoming an obligation. The same attention to context and clarity applies, but the pacing and language need to respect a different kind of moment.

decisions.question: How much introduction is enough?
decisions.options: Mandatory multi-step onboarding; optional overview; direct exploration.
decisions.reasoning: I would keep orientation short and allow exploration early. Guidance can appear again when it becomes relevant.
decisions.check: Whether people understand the offer and can choose a first activity without help.

decisions.question: How should the dashboard organize choices?
decisions.options: Content types; desired next action; personalized suggestions.
decisions.reasoning: I would test plain, distinct labels before adding personalization. Each label should set an understandable expectation.
decisions.check: Where people expect to find a particular activity, and why.

decisions.question: What makes a profile useful?
decisions.options: Lead with imagery and ratings; lead with relevant service details; combine both with clear hierarchy.
decisions.reasoning: I would prioritize the information needed to understand fit and the next action. Any credential or availability statement needs a dependable source.
decisions.check: What people need to know before sending a message or requesting a meeting.

decisions.question: What should progress communicate?
decisions.options: Time spent; completed activities; personal reflection.
decisions.reasoning: I would separate activity from wellbeing. A percentage of tasks completed should not imply a percentage of mental health achieved.
decisions.check: How people interpret the dashboard indicators and whether any wording creates unnecessary pressure.

about.Opening:
I work across business analysis, product ownership, and UX. What connects those disciplines for me is the effort to make a complex situation understandable: what someone is trying to do, what the business needs, and how the product should behave.

Financial and merchant products have made that relationship especially interesting to me. A balance needs an explanation. A payment needs a trustworthy status. A busy workflow needs a clear next action. Moodify extends that curiosity into a different setting: how a wellbeing experience can make the first step feel manageable.

I like moving between the larger product question and the small interaction that makes it real. This portfolio brings together selected work and reflections on those decisions.
about.How I approach the work: I start by making the question concrete. I map the journey, identify the business rules, and look for the points where different interpretations could lead to different behavior. I use flows and prototypes to make those decisions easier to discuss. When there is uncertainty, I want it visible enough that the team can choose what to investigate next.
about.The experience behind that perspective:
Selected contributions across financial and merchant products.

**Debt Ledger — Discovery to delivery**

I owned the work from discovery through delivery, mapping user journeys and translating them into business logic. The product shipped in two months across four sprints.

**mSeller — Business analysis and UX**

As Lead Business Analyst and UI/UX Designer, I simplified primary actions, developed animated onboarding, and worked on early dynamic QR integration for merchant workflows.

**BeeRich — Product ownership and analysis**

As Product Owner and Analyst, I worked on the connection between personal finance management and banking services and championed a unified dashboard.

**Moodify — Experience design study**

An exploration of onboarding, content discovery, practitioner profiles, and a personal wellbeing overview.
